chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Musa ibn Sa'dan from Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim from Hisham al-Jawaliqi who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Should I marry a woman for a mut'ah (temporary marriage) for a specific, indefinite period?' He said: 'That is more difficult for you; she inherits you and you inherit her, so it is not permissible for you to divorce her except after a period of purity and with two witnesses.' I said: 'May God improve you, then how should I marry her?' He said: 'For a numbered number of days, with a specified amount, according to what you have agreed upon. When her days are completed, her divorce is by virtue of the condition, and there is no maintenance for her upon you.' I said: 'What do we say to her?' He said: 'You say to her: I marry you upon the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and God is my guardian and your guardian, for such and such a month for such and such a dirham, on the condition that God guarantees for me that you will fulfill [the terms] for me, and I will not swear to you, nor will I claim your offspring, nor is there a waiting period for you upon me.' When your condition expires, do not marry until forty-five days have passed for you, and if childbirth occurs to you, inform me.'

key_terms.طُهْرٍ: Purity (state of being free from menstruation/post-natal bleeding)

ai.seo_question: What are the specific conditions for divorce and maintenance in temporary marriage (mut'ah) according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al-Isbasar details the contractual mechanics of mut'ah, emphasizing that the fixed term inherently constitutes the divorce, thereby exempting the husband from the formalities of talaq (purity/witnesses) and nafaqah (maintenance). It highlights the Shia juristic view that the 'waiting period' (iddah) is not a financial obligation but a biological necessity for lineage verification, as evidenced by the instruction to notify the husband if pregnancy occurs. This underscores the distinct legal status of mut'ah as a time-bound contract rather than a lifelong bond.
